Oil plunges 7% in a single session as Washington and Tehran leave the door to diplomacy ajar

On Monday, November 2, US crude (WTI) closed at $96.46, down 7.4% in one session, after the United States and Iran signalled they would give diplomacy a chance. Part of the “war premium” added to prices in October evaporated [1][2][3].
At midday in New York on Monday, November 2, Brent was at $104.66 (−7.7%) and WTI at $96.50 (−7.3%) [1][2].
At the close, WTI, the US benchmark, lost $7.66, or 7.36%, and settled at $96.46 a barrel [3].

The trigger: both sides signalled they would give diplomacy a chance. That wiped out part of the “war premium”, the extra price buyers pay when they fear running short of oil, which had lifted crude throughout October [2].
According to MoneyCheck, Iranian and Qatari officials were on a third day of talks on Monday about reopening the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of Gulf oil passed before the war [5].

Beware of comparisons: the December Brent contract expired on Friday, October 30, at $117.64; on Monday, quotes were already for the January contract, so a “7.7%” fall cannot be measured against $117.64 [4].

The relief is fragile: according to FXEmpire, prices bounced slightly in early Asian trading after reports of a US strike on Iran's island of Qeshm, which US officials describe as defensive, with Brent at $105.25 and WTI at $96.93 [6]. Goldman Sachs, for its part, raised its December Brent forecast to $105, from $90 previously [5].

Key takeaway: today the oil price measures less the number of barrels available than the probability that the Strait of Hormuz reopens. A simple diplomatic signal was enough to push WTI down by more than $7 in a day [2][3].

The mechanism is the war premium. When a strategic strait is blocked, buyers (refiners, states, traders) pay more to secure their deliveries. As soon as the threat seems to recede, that insurance becomes less useful and prices fall, even though not a single extra barrel has yet crossed the strait [2].

The fall can reverse just as fast. The bounce reported after the strike on Qeshm shows that a military incident is enough to bring the risk back into prices [6]. And even after Monday's drop, Brent is still around $100 a barrel: the world economy has not returned to pre-crisis prices [1][4].

For importing countries in Europe and Asia, the good news would be a lasting fall in fuel and gas prices. For producers the question is the opposite: the next milestone is the OPEC+ meeting on November 29, which is due to set 2027 output [7].

If you drive a diesel car or heat your home with fuel oil, a lasting fall in the barrel price eventually shows up at the pump, with a delay of a few weeks. But a single day of decline does not yet change posted prices: if the talks fail, the rise can come back just as quickly.

France: 10 million barrels of diesel leave state stocks to cut pump prices by 12 to 18 centimes

Since November 1, France has been releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from its strategic reserves, sold to distributors at their pre-crisis price. The government is aiming for a cut of 12 to 18 centimes a litre by January; TotalEnergies promises 8 to 12 centimes to private customers [1][2][4].
On October 7, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced that 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic stocks would be put on the market, sold to distributors at their pre-crisis price [1][3].
The decision follows the G7 agreement of October 2 to mobilise 100 million barrels of petroleum products from the strategic reserves of major economies [1].

The government says diesel prices will fall from November 1, by about 12 to 18 centimes a litre between November 2026 and January 2027 [1][4][5]. One motoring outlet speaks instead of 8 to 18 centimes: this is a state estimate, not an observed price [6].
TotalEnergies has pledged to cut its prices by 8 to 12 centimes for private customers and by 20 centimes for off-road diesel (GNR), used by building sites and farm machinery [2].
The 10 million barrels represent about a fifth of the country's strategic diesel stock [3].
Eligible companies can also apply, from November 2 to 30, for aid on off-road diesel of up to 20 centimes a litre, capped at €4,000 per company per month [7][8].

Key takeaway: faced with an expensive fuel, the state is dipping into its reserves to weigh on prices, a lever rarely used and one that does not last. It should be read as a boost of a few months, not a lasting solution [1][3].

The mechanism is simple: by selling 10 million barrels to distributors at their pre-crisis price, the state lets them buy part of their diesel more cheaply than on the market, and asks them to pass the saving on at the pump. Everything therefore depends on what distributors actually do with that advantage: no source yet quantifies the fall observed at stations [1][2][4].

The G7's choice to act together also matters: by releasing 100 million barrels of petroleum products, the major economies want to send a signal to markets, without replacing what the Gulf conflict has removed from supply [1]. A stock that has been sold is no longer there in the event of a new crisis: that is the price of the gesture.
For building sites and farms, the aid on off-road diesel (up to 20 centimes a litre, capped at €4,000 a month) aims to ease a bill that weighs directly on their costs [7][8].

If you drive a diesel, watch the prices posted at stations in the coming weeks: the promised cut is 12 to 18 centimes a litre, i.e. €6 to €9 saved on a 50-litre tank (a simple calculation from the government's range). If you see nothing move, you can compare several stations, as the cut is not passed on everywhere at the same pace.

news.2026-11-03-allemagne-gen-z-manifest: Germany: “Gen Z” protests against the cost of living turn violent in Berlin and Frankfurt, with dozens of arrests

On Saturday, October 31, more than 140,000 young people had registered to demonstrate in 23 German cities against the cost of living. The marches were followed by clashes: 56 arrests in Berlin, more than 30 in Frankfurt, and injured officers; police unions blame autonomous groups for the violence [2][3][4].

The “Gen Z regelt” (“Gen Z sorts it out”) initiative had called for simultaneous rallies on Saturday, October 31; more than 140,000 pupils and young people had registered online for 23 cities, and the organisers promised peaceful marches [4].
In Berlin, police announced 56 provisional arrests and 27 slightly injured officers; the march was halted early after stones and fireworks were thrown [3].
In Frankfurt, more than 30 people were detained in the evening and two weapons seized; in Cologne, five people were taken into custody and one person was injured [3].
According to broadcaster ZDF, Hesse's interior minister, Roman Poseck, spoke of “far more than 100 injured police officers”; Euronews Germany and ZDF describe violence and looting overnight [1][2].
Andreas Roßkopf, head of the federal police at the GdP union, judged that the Gen Z protests had turned out “very peaceful” and that the violence came from autonomous groups [2][3].

Before the day, Bavarian police had announced a “massive” presence to prevent riots, and police unions had warned of far-left influence; the movement draws inspiration from youth marches in France [5][6][8].
Key takeaway: the youth movement against the cost of living, born in France, has crossed the Rhine and takes a more violent form in Germany than its organisers had announced [1][2][6].

The cost of living is the common thread: the press links these marches to protests against the high cost of living, while France prepares for further marches [7]. What changes is the method: an initiative launched online, with no party or union, can bring tens of thousands of young people together in a few days, but the organisers do not control the stewarding. When a few groups seek confrontation, the whole movement is judged by them, even though the federal police itself acknowledges that most of the march was peaceful [2][3].

For the German government, the risk is political before it is economic: the debate shifts from purchasing power to public order, and each camp draws opposite arguments from it. The interior ministers of the Länder (Bavaria, Hesse) reacted on security, not on the demands [1][2][5].

If you travel to Germany or France in the coming days, check for marches planned in big cities: streets may be closed and transport disrupted. This movement also concerns you if you are a student: it is your generation on the streets, over prices that have risen faster than wages.

news.2026-11-03-bulgarie-yotova-elue-pre: Bulgaria: Iliana Yotova, seen as close to Moscow, elected president with 57.6% of the vote in a low-turnout runoff

On Sunday, November 1, Iliana Yotova won Bulgaria's presidential runoff with 57.6% of the vote, 343,601 votes ahead of her rival Andrey Gyurov (about 39.5%). She becomes the first woman elected head of state, in a country marked by the war in the Black Sea and the high cost of living [1][2][5].
According to the electoral commission's final results, the Iliana Yotova–Kiril Valchev ticket won 57.566% of the vote, 343,601 votes more than that of Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev [1].
Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, took about 39.5%; he conceded defeat as soon as the runoff polls closed [1][2][8].
Iliana Yotova becomes the first woman elected president of Bulgaria; she had been acting head of state since January, after Rumen Radev resigned to run in parliamentary elections [5][6].
In the first round on October 25, she had won only about 35% against 32% for Gyurov, with turnout of about 20%, a historic low [7][8].
In the runoff, turnout stayed low, according to Reuters, and about 2.95% of voters chose the “I support no one” option [1][2].

The campaign was about drone attacks on Black Sea shipping and economic hardship; the two finalists held different positions on Ukraine [7]. The Kyiv Independent describes Iliana Yotova as “Russia-friendly”, while the South China Morning Post calls her rival the pro-Western candidate [3][8].

Key takeaway: Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has just elected a president whom the Ukrainian press presents as close to Moscow, at a time when the Black Sea has become a danger zone for ships [3][7].

The result is wide (an 18-point lead), but low turnout qualifies the mandate: in the first round barely one voter in five turned out, and the runoff was also marked by weak turnout [1][2][8]. These scores mainly reflect weariness among an electorate tired of the cost of living and repeated political crises.

For the European Union, the question is whether Sofia stays aligned with sanctions on Russia and support for Ukraine. The presidential election does not alone decide government policy, but the president speaks for the country abroad, and her tone matters for Brussels as well as Kyiv [3][7].
The economic context weighs on the vote: the AP explicitly cites economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping among the themes of the campaign [7].

Bulgaria is a European Union country: if you travel there or have colleagues, business or family there, this vote shows a country divided over its relationship with Russia. For your daily life there is no immediate effect, but Sofia's positions matter in European votes on sanctions.

Australia raises its rate to 4.85%, the highest in 18 years, but the central bank board splits (6 votes to 3)

On Tuesday, November 3, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) raised its policy rate by 0.25 points to 4.85%, its highest level since late 2008. It is the fifth hike of 2026, decided by 6 votes to 3, as inflation reached 4.3% in September [1][2][3].
The RBA's monetary policy board raised the target rate by 25 basis points to 4.85%, “by majority”: six members in favour, three against [1][3].
It is the highest level since late 2008 and the fifth hike of the year, after a rate of 4.60% in September [2][4][8].
The bank justifies its decision by inflation, which reached 4.3% year on year in September, well above its 2–3% target range [1][2].
The RBA now expects inflation to stay above 3% for the coming year, until the end of 2027 according to its forecasts [1][3].
Its forecasts assume the rate rises by a further 35 basis points or so by mid-2027, in line with what markets expected, but the statement stops short of announcing further hikes [5][6].
For a borrower, a 0.25-point rise adds about A$92 a month on a A$600,000 mortgage over 25 years, if the lender passes it on in full [5]. The country's four big banks had forecast this hike [7].

Key takeaway: Australia is tightening credit while inflation refuses to ease, and the 6–3 vote shows the board is hesitating over what comes next. The RBA is thus continuing in November the hiking cycle begun in September [1][2][8].

The mechanism is classic: by making credit dearer, the central bank wants to slow household and business spending to bring inflation back towards 2–3%. The cost is immediate for borrowers, while the effect on prices takes time to arrive [5].

The message to markets is nuanced: the bank's forecasts assume a rise of about 35 basis points in the rate by mid-2027, in line with expectations, but the statement stresses data dependence and does not promise another hike [5][6]. The fact that three of nine members did not follow the majority suggests the end of the cycle is under discussion [1][3].
For readers outside Australia, this vote is a reminder: a central bank raises rates when inflation stays too strong, even if it costs borrowers, and even when its own board is divided.

If you live in Australia or have family there, your mortgage payment may rise by about a hundred Australian dollars. In France this decision changes nothing directly for your loan, but it shows that the fight against inflation is not over in rich countries.

Wall Street: the Nasdaq 100 enters a “correction” because of chips and AI, as oil collapses

On Monday, November 2, the Nasdaq 100 fell 1.4% to close at 27,989.82 points, more than 10% below its October 6 peak: what markets call a correction, the third of the year. Chips led the fall, while the Dow Jones benefited from lower oil [1][2][3].
The Nasdaq 100, the index of the hundred biggest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq, lost 1.4% on Monday, November 2, to close at 27,989.82 points [1][2].
It now stands more than 10% below its October 6 high, the threshold at which one speaks of a “correction”; it is the third of the year [1][2].
The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 3.4% on Monday, after a 7.2% plunge on Friday; it closed on Friday below its 200-day moving average for the first time since June 2025 [2][3].
According to Bloomberg, results from tech giants amplified fears about artificial-intelligence spending: investors wonder whether these investments will pay off enough [1][4].
Oracle, AMD and Marvell were among the biggest decliners of the session [5].
Conversely, the Dow Jones rose and the S&P 500 fell, as the oil price plunged on hopes of talks between Washington and Tehran [6].

Key takeaway: the engine of Wall Street for months, AI, is changing status, from promise to bill. When investors doubt that this spending will pay off enough, chip stocks, the most expensive, are the first to be sold [1][4].

A “correction” is not a crash: it is a fall of more than 10% from the last peak, without the market necessarily grinding to a halt. It indicates that buyers want a better price before returning, and can last a few weeks or a few months [1][2].

Chips are both the cause and the thermometer: an index that loses 7.2% on a Friday then 3.4% the following Monday shows sellers are in a hurry, and falling below the 200-day average, a level followed by many managers, can trigger automatic selling [2][3].

The link with geopolitics is direct: when oil falls 7% on hopes of a thaw with Iran, energy stocks fall back and fuel-consuming sectors breathe. That is what supported the Dow Jones while tech fell [6].

If your savings are in a global equity fund or an ETF that tracks big US stocks, part of your portfolio depends on these tech giants. A correction lowers the displayed value temporarily, and no one can say whether it will continue: we advise neither buying nor selling.

How it works: what is a stock-market “correction”?

When an index falls more than 10% from its recent high, it is called a correction. A share price reflects what investors expect of future profits: if those expectations fall, or if the price has risen too far, sellers outnumber buyers and the price drops. A technical threshold such as the 200-day moving average (the average price over the last 200 sessions) serves as a marker: falling below it pushes some funds to sell automatically, which amplifies the fall [1][2][3].

Apple beats expectations with $114.5 billion in sales, but memory-chip costs squeeze its margin and the share price falls

On Monday, November 2, Apple reported $114.5 billion in revenue for the July–September quarter, above expectations. But its chief financial officer warns that rising memory-chip prices will keep weighing, and the shares fell after the close [1][2][3].

Apple published on Monday, November 2, after Wall Street's close, revenue of $114.5 billion for its quarter ended in September, above analysts' expectations [1][3]; iPhone sales reached $57.58 billion [1][2].
Analysts were expecting about $113.3 billion in revenue and $1.99 in earnings per share; a year earlier, the equivalent quarter had brought in $102.5 billion [6].
Chief financial officer Kevan Parekh explained that more than 100% of the quarter-on-quarter change in gross margin was explained by the cost of memory chips [2][3].
Apple forecasts a gross margin of 47% to 48% for the December quarter, against 50.1% for the June quarter, and expects even higher memory costs; they will keep rising after December [2][3].
The company is aiming for revenue of $153.8 billion to $158.1 billion for the year-end quarter, up 7% to 10% [3].

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched at $1,199 and $1,299, $100 more than the equivalent iPhone 17 Pro models [3]. After the close, the shares fell by about 2% to 4% depending on the source; one site reports a bigger drop, others near-stability [3][4][5].

Key takeaway: Apple is selling more but earning less on each device, because memory chips, an essential component of the iPhone, cost more. That is why markets punish a company that nonetheless beats sales expectations [2][3].

The mechanism is understood through gross margin: the share of the selling price left after the cost of making the product. If components get dearer faster than product prices, that share falls, and profit with it, even when sales grow. Apple has already raised the price of its iPhone 18 Pro by $100, which shows it is passing part of the rise on to customers [2][3].

What worries investors is the duration: the company expects even higher memory costs in December and beyond, while its margin should be 47–48%, against 50.1% in the previous quarter [2][3]. For a group valued on its ability to deliver steady profits, three points of margin less weigh heavily on tens of billions of sales.
The November 2 session was already difficult for tech: the Nasdaq 100 entered a correction (see our story on it), and it was in this climate that Apple's results landed.

If you plan to change smartphone, expect higher prices: Apple has already raised its iPhone 18 Pro by $100, and memory costs more for the whole industry. If you hold Apple shares through a fund, a drop after the close says nothing about the long-term future: we explain, we advise neither buying nor selling.

How it works: why a company that beats expectations sees its share price fall

A share price reflects what investors expect of future profits, not just past results. When a company announces better-than-expected sales but warns that its costs will rise (here, memory), buyers revise future profits downward: the price can fall despite good figures. Gross margin (the selling price minus the cost of making the product) is watched closely, because a margin that falls three points on tens of billions of sales removes billions of profit [2][3].
